newsitem.title: UK: Maastricht Treaty may harm EMU in long term - CEPR.
newsitem.headline: Maastricht Treaty may harm EMU in long term - CEPR.

text.p: The long-term success of Europe's planned single currency could be jeopardised by the very criteria set out to define it, according to a report by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) .

The London-based CEPR, an independent think-tank, said that preoccupation with achieving short-run economic convergence -- like taking a one-off test -- may prompt single currency candidates to side-step important structural reforms in areas such as tax or labour market.

"The conditions do not necessarily commit policy-makers to making the kind of fundamental reforms which will ensure convergence in long-run economic performance," a paper presented for the CEPR at the Royal Economic Society Annual Conference said.

Under the Maastricht treaty governing the Economic and Monetary Union, meeting strict criteria on managing debt, inflation and foreign exchange in 1997 is a condition for joining the union from its start in 1999.

Taking inflation, which the Maastricht Treaty says must be within 1.5 percentage points of the average of the lowest three rates in Europe, the CEPR said wage settlements would tend to be moderate in anticipation of a tight monetary policy in the run-up to the union.
This added anti-inflationary effect of muted pay rises would then boost a potential entrant's credibility on price stability -- reducing the need for more fundamental reform, it said.

"Analysis ... shows that the presence of the entry condition can, paradoxically, induce the potential entrant to undertake less structural reform than it would do if entry to monetary union was unconditional," the report said.

"Entry into monetary union should be governed by convergence at a more fundamental level, relating to factors such as reform of tax systems or labour markets, which affect long-run economic performance." -- Kate Kelland, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7708
